## The paradox

_Eight reporters, each on their own beat. They read the same articles and tell you what they see — suggestion with citations, never proof of anyone's motive. When they split, the split is the story._

**Split.** hermes, hades, demeter pushed back; nemesis, dionysus checked out; janus, eros, persephone sat it out. Both readings stand — here is the whole split, nothing softened.

### Hermes — pushes back

_Beat: do the outlets' framings of the same event diverge, and what does the divergence hide?_

Same event, 6 outlets, 6 different front doors. Here is how each one leads it: Houston Public Media opens with "Trump promises $5,000 dividend in convention speech, but only if Republicans win"; Indiana Capital Chronicle opens with "Republicans attack ex-GOP Mayor Ballard in party’s opening secretary of state ad"; ap.org opens with "Democratic Sen. Fetterman speaks at a GOP midterm convention, fueling party-switch fears"; Houston Public Media opens with "GOP’s first midterm convention kicks off Wednesday, putting Dallas at center of national politics".

I read every version, and they are barely the same story. Houston Public Media wants you thinking about "Trump promises $5,000 dividend in convention speech, but only if Republicans win". Indiana Capital Chronicle wants you thinking about "Republicans attack ex-GOP Mayor Ballard in party’s opening secretary of state ad". ap.org wants you thinking about "Democratic Sen. Fetterman speaks at a GOP midterm convention, fueling party-switch fears". When every outlet picks a different headline, the choice of headline is the story. Read one and you will feel informed. Read them all and you will realize each one buried somebody else's lead.

**Why Hermes reads it this way:** My beat is framing: how the outlets choose to tell the same event. I pulled the key names and terms from each of the 6 outlets' headlines and compared them — only 27% overlapped, and my bar for "the same story" is 60%. Concretely: Houston Public Media leads with "Trump promises $5,000 dividend in convention speech, but only if Republicans win" while Indiana Capital Chronicle leads with "Republicans attack ex-GOP Mayor Ballard in party’s opening secretary of state ad". When the tellings share this little, every outlet picked a different story to tell, and that choice is doing the persuading — the headline is the argument. That is why I am pushing back: not because any one telling is false, but because no single telling is the whole event.
